Current Affairs Including General Knowledge
13.	Answer: C
Explanation: A) 1948 — Incorrect. 1948 was the year the University Education Commission
(Radhakrishnan Commission) was constituted; it only recommended forming the UGC, not the
year of its statutory establishment.
B) 1953 — Incorrect. The UGC was formally inaugurated in 1953 by Maulana Abul Kalam Azad,
but it was not yet backed by an Act of Parliament and hence not a statutory body at that point.
C) 1956 — Correct. Following the recommendation of the Radhakrishnan Commission, Parliament
enacted the University Grants Commission Act, 1956, giving the UGC statutory status. Its
mandate is to coordinate, determine, and maintain standards of teaching, examination, and
research in universities.
D) 1964 — Incorrect. 1964 is associated with the Kothari Commission (Education Commission,
1964-66), a separate landmark body that recommended reforms to the national education policy,
not the UGC's establishment.
14.	Answer: A
Explanation: A) Dr. S. Radhakrishnan — Correct. The University Education Commission of
1948, popularly known as the Radhakrishnan Commission, was chaired by Dr. Sarvepalli
Radhakrishnan — philosopher, statesman, and later the second President of India. It
recommended reconstituting the UGC on the lines of the University Grants Committee of the
United Kingdom.
B) Dr. D.S. Kothari — Incorrect. Dr. D.S. Kothari chaired the Education Commission of 1964-66
(Kothari Commission), which dealt with the broad restructuring of India's education system. He is
a distinct figure from the 1948 commission.
C) Zakir Hussain — Incorrect. Zakir Hussain was an eminent educationist and the third President
of India, closely associated with Jamia Millia Islamia, but he did not chair the 1948 University
Education Commission.
D) J.P. Naik — Incorrect. J.P. Naik was a notable education administrator and policy researcher
associated with NCERT and educational planning in India, but he had no role in chairing the 1948
commission.
15.	Answer: B
Reference Line: "As an interim measure, the Court stayed the 2026 regulations and allowed the
earlier 2012 framework to continue until further review.”
Explanation: A) 1 and 2 only — Incorrect. Statement 2 is true, but Statement 1 is false — the
Court did not remove all equity regulations; the earlier 2012 framework was expressly allowed to
continue in operation.
B) 2 and 3 only — Correct. Statement 2 is directly supported by the passage: the 2012 framework
was kept alive. Statement 3 is also supported: the Court 'acknowledged the importance of
addressing such issues' while questioning whether the new regulations might create further
divisions. Statement 1 is false because the 2012 framework continues to operate.
C) 1 and 3 only — Incorrect. Statement 1 is factually wrong — the earlier 2012 equity regulations
remained in force, so not all regulations were removed from operation.

D) 1, 2 and 3 Incorrect. As established, Statement 1 is incorrect, making any combination that

16.	Answer: B
Explanation: A) United States — Incorrect. India borrowed the phrase 'Equal protection of laws'
from the American Constitution — a positive concept that mandates active state action to ensure
equality. 'Equality before law,' however, is of British origin.
B) Britain — Correct. 'Equality before law' is a concept rooted in the British legal tradition,
associated with A.V. Dicey's theory of Rule of Law. It is a negative concept implying the absence of
any special privilege for any person. Both phrases — 'equality before law' (British) and ‘equal
protection of laws' (American) — together form Article 14 of the Indian Constitution.
C) Ireland — Incorrect. India borrowed the concept of Directive Principles of State Policy from the
Trish Constitution of 1937, not Article 14's concept of equality.
D) Canada — Incorrect. Canada's influence on the Indian Constitution is limited and does not
include the ‘equality before law' formulation of Article 14.
Ais	Answer: A
Reference Line: "Critics argued that this limited definition excluded students from the general
category and could violate the principle of equality guaranteed under Article 14 of the
Constitution.”
Explanation: A) It may neglect similar forms of unfair treatment faced by other
categories. — Correct. The passage explicitly states that critics argued the definition covering
only SC, ST, and OBC students excluded general category students, potentially violating Article
14's guarantee of equality. This supports the inference that the regulation risks ignoring unfair
treatment faced by students outside these groups.
B) It ensures swift resolution of all discrimination complaints. — Incorrect. The passage actually
highlights the absence of safeguards and the lack of mechanisms to address complaints,
particularly malicious ones — directly contradicting any inference about swift resolution.
C) It guarantees that only genuine cases are filed in institutions. — Incorrect. The passage
specifically raises concerns that the regulations had no clear mechanism to address false or
malicious complaints, undermining any claim that it filters out non-genuine cases.
D) It automatically equalises all opportunities across caste groups. — Incorrect. The passage
raises doubts about the regulation creating further divisions, not achieving automatic equalization
of opportunities across caste groups.
18.	Answer: B
Explanation: A) The USSR would lead global economic reforms — Incorrect. By 1991, the Soviet
Union had already collapsed, rendering it incapable of leading any global initiative. Bush's vision
was premised precisely on the end of Soviet power.
B) The UN would play a central role in conflict resolution — Correct. President Bush used
the phrase 'New World Order' to describe a post-Cold War era where the United Nations could
finally function as originally envisioned — as an effective collective security body, no longer
paralysed by the superpower rivalry and the Soviet veto that had deadlocked it for decades.
C) Military alliances like NATO would be disbanded — Incorrect. Far from being disbanded,
NATO expanded eastward after the Cold War. Bush's 'New World Order' was about multilateral
cooperation through the UN, not the dismantling of alliances.

D) Third-world nations would gain veto power in the UN — Incorrect. No such restructuring of the
UN Security Council's veto arrangement occurred or was proposed by Bush. Veto power has
remained exclusively with the five permanent members.
19.	Answer: B
Explanation: A) The Molotov Plan — Incorrect. The Molotov Plan (1947) was an economic aid
programme through which the Soviet Union provided assistance to Central and Eastern European
satellite states. It was an economic arrangement, not a military alliance.
B) The Warsaw Pact — Correct. The Warsaw Pact (Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation and
Mutual Assistance, 1955) was the collective defence treaty signed among the Soviet Union and
seven Eastern European satellite states. It was the direct military counterpart to NATO and was
dissolved in 1991 following the collapse of the Soviet bloc.
C) The SEATO Treaty — Incorrect. SEATO (Southeast Asia Treaty Organization) was a US-
backed anti-communist collective defence arrangement for the Asia-Pacific region, entirely
separate from the Eastern European NATO—Warsaw Pact dynamic.
D) The COMECON Agreement — Incorrect. COMECON (Council for Mutual Economic Assistance)
was the Soviet-led economic organisation for socialist states — an economic body, not a military
one.
20.	Answer: B
Reference Line: "A coalition of around 660,000 troops from 34 countries was formed, but the
operation was largely dominated by the US. Led by American General Norman Schwarzkopf,
nearly 75% of the forces belonged to the US."
Explanation: A) The war showed that collective action was possible without any US involvement.
— Incorrect. The passage explicitly states that approximately 75% of coalition forces were
American and the operation was ‘largely dominated by the US,' making this inference the opposite
of what the passage establishes.
B) The war underlined that US military power was central even in UN-backed
operations. — Correct. With nearly 75% of the 660,000-strong coalition forces being American
and the operation commanded by a US General, the passage clearly establishes that even a
multilateral, UN-authorised coalition was predominantly a US military enterprise, reinforcing
American dominance.
C) The war proved that small states alone could enforce UN resolutions. — Incorrect. The passage
highlights the dominance of the US — a superpower — in the operation. There is no evidence to
suggest that small or medium-sized states drove the enforcement of the UN mandate.
D) The war established that the UN had its own standing army. — Incorrect. The UN does not
maintain an independent standing army. The coalition was formed by member states who
contributed forces; the UN merely authorised the operation.
21.	Answer: B
Explanation: A) Hezbollah — Incorrect. Hezbollah is a Lebanese Shia militant and political
organisation founded in 1982 with Iranian support. It has no connection to Iraq's Ba'athist
governance.

B) Ba'ath Party — Correct. Saddam Hussein was a leading member of the Arab Socialist Ba'ath
Party (Iraqi faction), whose ideology — Ba'athism — combined Arab nationalism and socialism. A
separate faction of the same party governed Syria under the Assad family for decades.
C) Muslim Brotherhood — Incorrect. The Muslim Brotherhood is a Sunni Islamist organisation
with roots in Egypt (founded 1928). It is ideologically distinct from the secular, pan-Arab
nationalist Ba'ath Party.
D) Al-Dawa Party — Incorrect. Al-Dawa is an Iraqi Shia Islamist party that was actually brutally
suppressed by Saddam Hussein's Ba'athist government. It represents a completely different
ideological tradition.
22.	Answer: C
Reference Line: "some of its foundations had already been laid after the end of Second World
War in 1945. However, the US did not immediately act as a hegemonic power; it gradually assumed
this role over time."
Explanation: A) It began immediately after the Second World War ended in 1945. — Incorrect.
The passage clearly states the US 'did not immediately act as a hegemonic power,' directly
negating any claim of immediate post-1945 hegemonic behaviour.
B) It clearly began only after the First Gulf War ended in 1991. — Incorrect. The passage states
that foundations were laid after 1945 — well before the Gulf War — making a 1991-only starting
point inaccurate.
C) Its foundations were laid after 1945, but it emerged gradually and became evident by
the time of the First Gulf War. — Correct. This option captures all three dimensions the
passage presents: (i) some foundations were built post-1945; (ii) the US ‘gradually assumed' its
hegemonic role; and (iii) the First Gulf War served as a major demonstration of that growing
dominance. No single sharp starting point is indicated.
D) It began only after the collapse of the Soviet Union, with no earlier foundations. — Incorrect.
The passage explicitly contradicts this by stating that 'some of its foundations had already been
laid after the end of Second World War in 1945."
23.	Answer: B
Reference Line: "the mission carried four astronauts aboard the Orion spacecraft on a 10-day
journey around the Moon."
Explanation: A) Dragon — Incorrect. SpaceX's Dragon spacecraft is used for crew and cargo
missions to the International Space Station in low Earth orbit. It is not designed for deep-space or
lunar missions.
B) Orion — Correct. The passage directly states that the crew was ‘carried aboard the Orion
spacecraft.'! NASA's Orion Multi-Purpose Crew Vehicle is specifically designed for deep-space
exploration and is launched atop the Space Launch System (SLS) rocket. Artemis I tested it
without a crew; Artemis II is its first crewed mission.
C) Starliner — Incorrect. Boeing's CST-100 Starliner is designed solely for crew transport to the
ISS in low Earth orbit. It has no role in lunar or deep-space missions under the Artemis
programme.
D) Cygnus — Incorrect. Northrop Grumman's Cygnus is an uncrewed cargo spacecraft used
exclusively for ISS resupply missions. It cannot carry astronauts or travel to the Moon.

LAW PREP

24.	Answer: B
Explanation: A) First person to walk on Mars — Incorrect. No human has walked on Mars as of
2026. Mars exploration remains a goal for future missions.
B) Longest single spaceflight by a woman — Correct. Christina Koch spent 328 days
continuously aboard the International Space Station during her mission from March 2019 to
February 2020, setting the record for the longest single spaceflight by a woman at that time.
C) First woman to command a Space Shuttle — Incorrect. The Space Shuttle programme was
retired in 2011. Koch was not a Shuttle astronaut, let alone a Shuttle commander.
D) Youngest person to enter Earth's orbit — Incorrect. The record for youngest person to orbit
Earth is not associated with Christina Koch. She is recognised for mission duration, not age-
related records.
25.	Answer: C
Explanation: A) Mercury — Incorrect. Project Mercury (1958-1963) was NASA's first human
spaceflight programme; its sole objective was to place a human in Earth orbit and safely return
them. It had no lunar component.
B) Gemini — Incorrect. Project Gemini (1961-1966) was a bridge programme between Mercury
and Apollo, designed to test spacewalking, docking, and long-duration spaceflights. It prepared
astronauts for the Moon but did not attempt a landing.
C) Apollo — Correct. NASA's Apollo programme (1961-1972) accomplished the first crewed lunar
landing. Apollo 11, on 20 July 1969, saw Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin become the first humans
to walk on the Moon, while Michael Collins orbited overhead.
D) Skylab — Incorrect. Skylab was America's first space station, operational from 1973 to 1979. It
focused on scientific experiments in Earth orbit and had no involvement in lunar landings.
26.	Answer: A
Explanation: A) Merritt Island — Correct. The John F. Kennedy Space Center (KSC) is located
on Merritt Island, Brevard County, Florida, adjacent to Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. It
has been the primary launch centre for American human spaceflight since 1968, including the
Apollo missions and now Artemis.
B) Key West — Incorrect. Key West is a city located at the southernmost tip of Florida —
approximately 500 km south of the launch complex — and has no connection to NASA operations.
C) Amelia Island — Incorrect. Amelia Island is a barrier island in Nassau County, northeastern
Florida. It is known as a resort destination and has no space launch infrastructure.
D) Sanibel Island — Incorrect. Sanibel Island is a resort island on Florida's southwest Gulf Coast,
far from the Atlantic coast where KSC is located.
27.	Answer: B
Reference Line: "The astronauts conducted a lunar flyby, capturing images of the Moon's far
side... the spacecraft safely returned to Earth with a successful splashdown in the Pacific Ocean."
Explanation: A) A complete landing and surface exploration on the Moon before returning to
Earth. — Incorrect. The passage makes no mention of a Moon landing. Artemis II was a test
mission for systems and navigation; a crewed landing is the goal of a future Artemis mission.

B) A brief pass around the Moon, including its far side, without landing, after which the
spacecraft returns to Earth. — Correct. The passage states the crew conducted a ‘lunar flyby,
capturing images of the Moon's far side' and subsequently 'the spacecraft safely returned to Earth
with a successful splashdown in the Pacific Ocean.' This confirms a trajectory that looped around
the Moon without landing before returning to Earth.
C) Parking the spacecraft in permanent orbit around the Moon to serve as a future station. —
Incorrect. The passage clearly states the spacecraft returned to Earth after the flyby. No
permanent lunar orbit or station was established during Artemis II.
D) Sending an uncrewed probe to circle the Moon while the astronauts remain in Earth orbit. —
Incorrect. The passage establishes that the four named astronauts themselves were aboard the
Orion spacecraft during the lunar flyby; no separation between the crewed capsule and an
uncrewed probe is described.
28.	Answer: A
Explanation: A) Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram — Correct. The Sixth Schedule
(read with Article 244) specifically applies to the tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and
Mizoram — often remembered by the acronym AMTM. It provides for the creation of Autonomous
District Councils (ADCs) in these states to protect tribal rights. Ladakh's demand for Sixth
Schedule inclusion would, if granted, extend these protections to a Union Territory for the first
time.
B) Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur, and Mizoram — Incorrect. Arunachal Pradesh and
Nagaland have special provisions under Articles 371B and 371A respectively, but are not covered
by the Sixth Schedule. Only Mizoram from this list is a Sixth Schedule state.
C) Assam, Nagaland, Manipur, and Tripura — Incorrect. Nagaland and Manipur fall under
separate constitutional provisions (Articles 371A and 371C). Assam and Tripura are correct, but
replacing Meghalaya and Mizoram with Nagaland and Manipur makes this option wrong.
D) Meghalaya, Mizoram, Manipur, and Arunachal Pradesh — Incorrect. While Meghalaya and
Mizoram are correctly included, Manipur and Arunachal Pradesh are not covered under the Sixth
Schedule. This option incorrectly omits Assam and Tripura.
29.	Answer: B
Explanation: A) Zila Parishads — Incorrect. Zila Parishads are district-level elected bodies under
the Panchayati Raj system (Article 243), which applies broadly to rural local governance. They are
distinct from the special Autonomous District Councils established under the Sixth Schedule.
B) Autonomous District Councils (ADCs) — Correct. The Sixth Schedule empowers
Autonomous District Councils (ADCs) — elected bodies in tribal areas — with legislative, judicial,
and executive authority. They can make laws on land management, forests, use of waterways,
shifting cultivation, establishment of village or town administration, inheritance of property,
marriage and divorce, and money-lending, subject to the Governor's assent.
C) Gram Sabhas — Incorrect. Gram Sabhas are village assemblies at the grassroots level under
the Panchayati Raj framework. They have consultative and participatory roles, not the broad
legislative and judicial powers granted to ADCs under the Sixth Schedule.

LAW PREP
— Tutorial—	MOCK CLAT 10020 : ANSWER & EXPLANATIONS
D) Tribal Advisory Councils — Incorrect. Tribal Advisory Councils are bodies constituted under
the Fifth Schedule (applicable to Scheduled Areas in states other than the four Sixth Schedule
states) to advise on the welfare of Scheduled Tribes. They are advisory, not legislative bodies.
30.	Answer: A
Explanation: A) R.K. Mathur — Incorrect. R.K. Mathur served as the first Lieutenant Governor
of Ladakh from October 2019 to February 2023. He was succeeded by B.D. Mishra and is no longer
in the post.
B) VK Saxena— Correct. As of March 13, 2026, Vinai Kumar Saxena is the 4th and incumbent
Lieutenant Governor of the Union Territory of Ladakh. A former Lieutenant Governor of Delhi, he
took oath following the resignation of his predecessor, Kavinder Gupta. Saxena, known for his
administrative experience in structural reforms, was appointed by President Droupadi Murmu
and is focused on improving tourism potential, enhancing infrastructure, and fostering sustainable
development in the region. He resides and operates from the Raj Niwas in Leh.
C) Manoj Sinha — Incorrect. Manoj Sinha is the Lieutenant Governor of the Union Territory of
Jammu and Kashmir, not Ladakh. Ladakh and J&K are separate UTs since the Jammu and
Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019.
D) Praful Khoda Patel — Incorrect. Praful Khoda Patel has served as the LG of Dadra and Nagar
Haveli and Daman and Diu. He has no association with the Ladakh administration.
31.	Answer: B
Explanation: A) Khardung La — Incorrect. Khardung La (approximately 17,582 ft) was long
marketed as the world's highest motorable pass, but this claim has since been superseded by the
BRO's Umling La road. Khardung La is significant but no longer holds the top record.
B) Mig La — Correct. As of 2026, the Mig La Pass is the highest motorable pass in the world,
reaching an altitude of 19,400 feet (5,913 metres). Located in the Eastern Ladakh sector, this pass
was constructed by the Border Roads Organisation (BRO) under Project Himank. It officially
surpassed the previous world record held by the Umling La Pass, which stands at 19,024 feet.
C) Nathu La — Incorrect. Nathu La (approximately 14,140 ft) is a mountain pass in Sikkim on the
India-China border. It is not located in Ladakh and is far below the altitude of either Khardung La
or Umling La.
D) Zoji La — Incorrect. Zoji La (approximately 11,575 ft) is a strategic pass connecting Srinagar to
the Kargil-Leh region. While important as a gateway to Ladakh, it is nowhere near the altitude of
the highest motorable passes.
32.	Answer: B
Reference Line: "many residents have expressed concerns over reduced political representation
and lack of legislative powers."
Explanation: A) They are primarily worried about an excessive concentration of legislative
powers in a local assembly. — Incorrect. The protesters' concern is precisely the opposite —
Ladakh as a UT without a legislature has too little legislative power. The demand is for more
representation, not less.
B) They believe Union Territory status has reduced their political voice and control
over local resources. — Correct. The passage states that since becoming a UT in 2019, 'many
residents have expressed concerns over reduced political representation and lack of legislative

LAW PREP
— Tutorial—	MOCK CLAT 10020 : ANSWER & EXPLANATIONS
powers.’ The protesters demand statehood and Sixth Schedule protections precisely to regain
control over land, employment, and cultural heritage.
C) They feel the present arrangement gives too much autonomy to locally elected bodies. —
Incorrect. Ladakh's UT status provides no elected legislature at all. The protests are about the
absence of autonomy, not its excess.
D) They are mainly demanding the merger of Ladakh back with Jammu and Kashmir. —
Incorrect. The passage clearly states that protesters demand full statehood and Sixth Schedule
inclusion — both of which would strengthen Ladakh's independent constitutional standing. A
merger with J&K is not among the stated demands.
33.	Answer: C
Explanation: A) ISRO — Incorrect. The Indian Space Research Organisation focuses on space
science, satellite development, and launch vehicles. While some of its technology has dual-use
applications, ISRO is not the primary body for weapons-system R&D.
B) HAL — Incorrect. Hindustan Aeronautics Limited is primarily a manufacturing PSU — it
builds aircraft and helicopters — not a research and development organisation responsible for
missile or weapons design.
C) DRDO — Correct. The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), functioning
under the Ministry of Defence, is India's apex defence R&D body. It has developed strategic
systems such as the Agni ballistic missiles, Akash surface-to-air missiles, Tejas fighter aircraft,
and Arjun main battle tank, among others.
D) BEL — Incorrect. Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL) manufactures defence electronics, radars,
and communication systems. It primarily commercialises and produces systems developed by
DRDO and is not a core weapons R&D body.
34.	Answer: C
Explanation: A) France — Incorrect. India's notable defence cooperation with France includes
the Rafale fighter jets and Scorpéne-class submarines. The BrahMos missile is not part of the
India-France defence partnership.
B) Israel — Incorrect. India-Israel defence cooperation spans UAVs (drones), radar systems, and
missiles such as Barak and Spyder air defence systems, but not the BrahMos.
C) Russia — Correct. BrahMos Aerospace is a joint venture between India's DRDO and Russia's
NPO Mashinostroyeniya. The name 'BrahMos' is derived from the Brahmaputra River (India) and
the Moskva River (Russia). It is among the world's fastest supersonic cruise missiles in service.
D) United States — Incorrect. The US has no role in the BrahMos joint venture. In fact,
discussions around transferring BrahMos to US partners or allies are a separate geopolitical issue
from the missile's development origin.
35.	Answer: B
Explanation: A) China — Incorrect. China is among the world's largest arms exporters. It ranks
well below India as an arms importer, given China's advanced domestic defence manufacturing
capability.
B) India — Correct. SIPRI has consistently ranked India as the world's single largest importer of
major arms over multiple years. The Government of India's 'Atmanirbhar Bharat' (Self-Reliant

LAW PREP

India) initiative is directly aimed at reversing this trend by boosting domestic defence
manufacturing and growing exports.
C) Saudi Arabia — Incorrect. Saudi Arabia is consistently among the world's top arms importers,
but has not held the position of the single largest importer as consistently as India has over the
past decade.
D) Pakistan — Incorrect. Pakistan is a significant arms importer, but its total volume is far
smaller than India's, which has traditionally dominated the top spot on SIPRI's importer
rankings.
36.	Answer: C
Explanation: A) Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL) — Incorrect. BEL specialises in defence
electronics, including radars, communication systems, electronic voting machines, and sonar
devices. Aircraft manufacturing is outside its domain.
B) Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders (MDL) — Incorrect. MDL is a premier shipbuilding PSU under the
Ministry of Defence, responsible for constructing naval submarines (including Scorpéne class) and
warships — not aircraft.
C) Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) — Correct. HAL is India's premier aerospace PSU
under the Ministry of Defence. It manufactures and maintains several platforms including the
Tejas Light Combat Aircraft (LCA), Dhruv Advanced Light Helicopter, Prachand Light Combat
Helicopter, and Sukhoi Su-30MKI under licence.
D) Bharat Dynamics Limited (BDL) — Incorrect. BDL is a defence PSU that manufactures
missiles, torpedoes, and underwater weapons. It is not involved in aircraft manufacturing.
37.	Answer: A
Explanation: A) Sukumar Sen — Correct. Sukumar Sen, an Indian Civil Service officer, served
as India's first Chief Election Commissioner from 1950 to 1958. He is widely credited with
successfully organising India's first two general elections (1951-52 and 1957) — massive logistical
and democratic undertakings involving hundreds of millions of voters, largely illiterate, across a
newly independent nation.
B) Kalyan Sundaram — Incorrect. Kalyan Sundaram served as the 8th Chief Election
Commissioner of India (1977-1982). He was not the first CEC.
C) T.N. Seshan — Incorrect. T.N. Seshan served as the 10th CEC from 1990 to 1996 and is
